sentences.text: The name Acrotholus translates to "highest dome" in Greek, reflecting its most striking feature.
Unlike most members of its group, this dinosaur possessed an oval-shaped skull cap that reached a maximum thickness of 55 millimeters.
A prominent ridge runs along the center of the rear section of the top skull bones.
The lack of specific surface bumps suggests the individual preserved was either fully grown or nearly so.
These creatures were surprisingly small, with an estimated body length of 1.5 to 2 meters and a weight of only 40 kilograms.
Fossil records show that about two-thirds of known specimens are known solely from their skulls.
The genus was formally named by Evans and colleagues in 2013 based on a fossil found in 2008.
This small skull was unearthed at the edge of the Milk River in Southern Alberta, located one mile east of the Provincial Writing-on-Stone.
Scientists generally believe the thickened head served as a weapon for fighting members of the same species.
Studies of related species reveal bone diseases similar to those seen in modern mammals that engage in physical contact.
Evidence of healed injuries on several skulls indicates that individuals survived encounters involving their heads.
Analyses of limb proportions suggest these animals lived near wetlands, similar to modern moose and wading birds.
Acrotholus is recognized as one of the earliest confirmed members of the pachycephalosaur family.
It is classified as a sister group to Prenocephale, forming a branch distinct from other genera like Pachycephalosaurus.
The taxon belongs to the subfamily Pachycephalosaurinae and the family Pachycephalosauridae.
This animal lived approximately 84 million years ago during the Late Cretaceous Santonian stage.
The geological formation where it was found exposes organisms from the Late Santonian, and analysis suggests many such species inhabited coastal regions.
